records.title: Show HN: Kairos – Open-source risk and fraud decisioning platform
records.author: ayanb9440
records.storyText:
Hey HN, Ayan here from Finic. We’re launching Kairos, an open source alternative to Sift, Sardine, and other real-time fraud decisioning platforms. Kairos addresses two of the biggest problems facing traditional decisioning tools: a lack of labeled data to train on and dealing with fraudsters that are constantly changing their tactics.

1. Traditional fraud solutions use ML models such as XGBoost to detect fraud, but these models are dependent on quality labeled data which many businesses do not have. We address this by using “System One” decision models in additional to traditional models such as XGBoost and logistic regression. This allows you to incorporate plain language questions such as “Is this a throwaway email” into your decisioning, bypassing the need for large amounts of labeled data. This also allows you to capture aspects of fraud that are more unstructured, which is something that XGBoost models struggle with.

2. Fraud teams are facing off with live players that are constantly changing their behavior to bypass the detection logic they have in place. You can train a detection model or define a ruleset once, but it will become obsolete in a matter of weeks as fraudsters figure out what your detection logic is. This means that you need a team regularly training models and updating rules based on new fraud patterns. Typically this takes a large data science/ML team. Kairos addresses this by introducing an MCP server, so that your agent (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, etc.) can define a decision workflow, train models on your data, and pick the variant that performs best.

You can self-host Kairos with Docker or use the hosted version at https://kairos.finic.ai

records.title: Show HN: Spooler – a simple, managed message queue
records.author: gobwas
records.storyText:
Hi Folks,

I'm Sergey, founder of Spooler (https://spooler.sh) -- a durable, fully managed message queue, inspired by the simplicity of Go channels.

Why? Whenever I needed a queue for something, it often felt that adding one would be a bigger project than the solution. Existing systems offered far more than I needed, while using a relational database usually meant inventing queue semantics on the go.

What I really wanted was just a send and recv with retries.

After nearly six months of engineering, I'm really happy to share the result with you.

How it works: you send a message to the queue, you recv it leased; when the message processing is done you acknowledge it, if the lease times out, the message gets back to the queue to be delivered again or into the failed state on too many retries.

There is an atomic ack-and-send: you can acknowledge a message and append another in a single operation. You can model state machines with it: a queue is a state, a message in the queue is an object in that state, and ack-and-send is the transition.

Each Spooler queue lives in a spool: a storage isolation unit (hence the product name) with its own write-ahead log and replication. That means that durable operations succeed only after the log entry is durable on disk and confirmed by the required number of replicas.

Feel free to try it out! There is a docker image for testing it locally: https://docs.spooler.sh/local (it uses the same API but with in-memory storage, which means messages live only as long as the container runs).

Spooler has an open-source CLI and Go library and there is also a repo of agent skills for it. The server itself is closed source, so there is no self-hosted options today.

Please do share your thoughts about the product -- I really hope it feels ordinary to use.

Sergey.

records.author: vatsaltanna
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

I made this to help improve visualisation for a meditation I practise where you picture leaving your body moving outward in stages until you are beyond space-time. It’s helped me get through some really tough times by putting things in perspective.

You start as a skeleton by the pyramids at Giza and scroll past Earth, the planets, the stars, the Milky Way and the galaxy clusters to the edge of the observable universe.

It’s built with real data - 9,096 stars (Yale Bright Star Catalogue), 43,463 galaxies (2MASS Redshift Survey), asteroids (JPL), Earth (NASA Blue Marble) and Giza (Sentinel-2). The cosmic web and the faintest galaxies are generated.

Runs in the browser with three.js and WebGL 2 with no sign-up or tracking. Images are GPU-compressed and load only near their stage which cut peak GPU memory from 1.1 GB to 258 MB.

Hope you have fun playing around and would love to hear what you’d like to see more of!

records.title: Show HN: 8 years of "Who's Hiring?" in charts (hiring boom, bust, and AI trends)
records.author: LanceJones
records.storyText:
After seeing Andrej's HackerTube post (and given my sons are both junior-mid developers) I decided to point Codex at 8 years of "Who's hiring?" posts and rip through some tokens on semantic analysis of all that content. I started pre-COVID, thru October 2026, and the data was retrieved via HN API data.

5 things that stand out:

1. AI is now in half the posts. AI or machine learning appeared in 50% of 2026 posts, up from 17% in 2019.

2. Most employers posted in only one month. Across all 94 monthly threads, 53% of the employers we identified appeared in just one month.

3. Frontend roles fell from 16% to 3% of posts. That’s a substantial shift in the kinds of developers companies explicitly say they’re looking for.

4. Staff-level posts grew 3.6×. Posts naming staff-level roles rose from 77 in 2019 to 277 in 2026, even as the hiring board got smaller.

5. Only 41 posts explicitly named junior roles in 2026. Out of 2,932 posts. In 2019, there were 163.

... plus 20 other trends.

It feels like there's plenty to consider and discuss. Hope it's useful.

records.title: Show HN: Modelpeers – a changelog for the AI models and agents you use
records.author: liorgrossman
records.storyText:
Earlier this year, I had one of my product's features down for 48 hours because Anthropic retired Claude 3 Haiku. In another instance, an API parameter started returning errors.

I grew sick of not being able to follow and track the endless changes of AI models every week, so I decided to build Modelpeers. It's basically a feed of all these changes. You can follow models and agents that you use to see what is changing and what you need to do about it. Optionally, you can sign up to get a digest for the models/agents you follow.

Every few hours, it downloads and hashes dozens of pages from the prominent AI companies' pages, like changelogs, deprecation pages, status pages, and pricing pages. Then when a page changes, it pulls the diff, validates it with two models, and if validated as true, it posts it to the feed.

The feed currently has about 400 changes, 21 of them breaking changes.

Fun fact (well, not really fun): OpenAI alone has 12 shutdowns/cutoff planned for the next six months.

Would love to hear what y'all think.

records.title: Show HN: Confetti – Start designing hardware with plain English prompts
records.author: enaic
records.storyText:
Hey HN! We're Tianyi and Lucas from Confetti (YC F26) (https://confetti.build/). We’re building a platform that helps you turn your ideas into physical things using plain English.

Take a look at a quick demo video here: https://youtu.be/UhtAs4mg5O8

Making hardware has always required layers of expertise: learning modeling software, sourcing compatible components, designing enclosures, wiring, firmware, and finding someone to manufacture it all.

We experienced this firsthand while prototyping a home AI device we wanted to build. We didn't have too much experience in hardware and every step opened up more questions.

We spent so much time figuring out the process before we could make progress on the thing itself, so we built Confetti to make it easier to get started.

Confetti puts the whole process on one platform, driven by natural language:

- CAD: generate and edit 3D designs from text or image prompts

- Electronics: automatic sourcing for compatible off-the-shelf parts, wiring, and firmware

- Manufacturing: get quotes and place orders to get parts sent straight to your doorstep

- Community: share, remix, and personalize builds from other makers for yourself

In the same way that AI has made it much easier for people to build software, we think that we can use AI to enable a lot more people to start building the ideas they have for physical projects too.

We would love to hear feedback that you have, what sort of bugs and issues you run into, and features you'd like to see!

https://confetti.build/

records.title: Show HN: A browser studio with a SPICE-modeled Juno 106 (playing Nightcall)
records.author: tonioab
records.storyText:
I wanted the feeling of sitting down with a small "DAWless" hardware setup: a synth, some drums, a midi recorder, and knobs to turn. Something you can open for a quick jam, with enough care put into the sound that you’ll want to keep playing. The spirit is close to a DAWless setup, with the convenience of a browser tab.

The linked demo is a recreation of Kavinsky’s Nightcall. It opens as a playable session, so you can listen, explore the instruments, and change the sounds yourself. All the audio is generated locally in your browser.

I spent 80% of the dev time on Cybelle, a clone of the Juno-106, with a C++/WebAssembly sound engine. It was built with a SPICE model (model of the original circuit), which I then calibrated against my real hardware Juno. Reproducing the filter and the chorus took many iterations and blind tests, and I believe it strikes a good balance of audio fidelity and CPU performance for most laptops. To my ears, the Juno presets and filter sweeps sound the same between my hardware and Cybelle (as in, I can't differentiate them in blind tests).

An interesting side-effect of using "hill-climbing" agentic loops to optimize the sound engine is that I ended up spending hours on the UI as well, trying to make it immersive and photo-realistic.

I’d especially love feedback from people who make music with hardware: how does it sound, how does it feel to play, and what would make you reach for it when you have a few minutes to make music?

records.title: Show HN: Mallard: Git for the age of AI agents
records.author: rika321
records.storyText:
We started Mallard to make it easier to share our agent sessions and build things together. We spend much of our working day talking to Claude and Codex. Those conversations include the ideas, designs, and decisions behind our work. However they often stay on one machine, without backups or an easy way to share them.

3 months. 10 accounts on 20× plans. 100 billion tokens later, Mallard finally hatched.

Share and back up agent sessions using Cloudflare R2, Dropbox, or Mallard Cloud.

Explore the discussions and design decisions behind PRs, including Mallard’s hatching logs.

Pull and resume sessions in Codex or Claude Code with the original context.

For teams, Anthropic internally uses cloud VMs and Claude Tag so that teammates can work in shared agent conversations and pick up where others left off. Mallard lets teams achieve the same goal at almost zero cost, without any cloud VMs.

We want Mallard to be free and easy to use for everyone, rich or poor.

We built a lightweight version of GIT and reworked our storage protocol, removing CAS so Mallard can work with any cloud storage that supports LIST and PUT APIs. Bring your own storage or use Mallard Cloud. No Git server or expensive sandbox required.

We also added one-click sign-in for Dropbox and Cloudflare R2, so anyone can connect their own cloud storage to Mallard in just a few clicks.

We don’t think the internet, recommendation algorithms, or AI should be in the hands of just a few people. We hope Mallard helps more people share their work, find an audience, and have their voices heard.

Free and MIT licensed. Available on macOS and Windows. Website: https://mallard-ai.com/ GitHub: https://github.com/Git4Agent/mallard-app

records.title: Show HN: Oathshaper – A BioWare Inspired Open RPG Game Engine
records.author: azurewraith
records.storyText:
Hey HN!

I’ve been building an open RPG game engine called Oathshaper. It’s current incarnation was created with Godot and inspired by the BioWare classics (Jade Empire, Mass Effect, Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age, etc.) The storytelling, voice acting and actions that have consequences in those games have always found a place in my heart.

A few weeks back I was showing my son how each BioWare game had different combat mechanics on a Steam Deck and I was inspired to create Oathshaper to model these mechanisms around a cohesive, voice driven story telling foundation. A short time later we heard the news that the BioWare studio was closing.

The game engine is written in Rust which hooks into Godot

I’ve released it as MIT on GitHub - https://github.com/oathshaper/oathshaper - free for the world to explore and collaborate on. It includes some tooling aimed at educators looking to teach AI/Agentic forward game design. An introductory game design course/offering could let students design their own storyboard implementation with assets as the first project and spend the rest of the curriculum going back and learning how each part of the asset/content creation pipeline actually works.

records.title: Show HN: An ant simulation whose search walk is tested against real ant tracks
records.author: hokapo
records.storyText:
I've been building an ant simulation that runs in the browser, and thought maybe someone would have fun playing around with it for a few minutes.

I always stop and look at ant colonies when I go past them in nature, and thought it would be fun to try to simulate them. I was inspired by Sebastian Lague's and Pezzza's Work's ant videos. I first made this quite advanced simulation with food, predators, competing colonies, queens making new colonies, and hunger. But then I started thinking how realistic it is, and it sent me down a rabbit hole, finding research papers on the topic, and making a model of how real ants walk in real-life experiments.

The "realistic" walk is on by default, and you can turn it off to see how it compares to a random walk. The research paper I got the real ant data from showed that the ants' walks aren't a simple random walk, by comparing the times they cross their own path to that of a random walk, and I took their ideas and metrics further when making my own model. It's not perfect, but I'd say it's good enough for now. For now I focused only on the walking patterns when the ants are searching for food, and not on how they follow pheromone trails or how they find their way home. Those are educated guesses in the simulation, but maybe I'll try to replicate real ant behaviour on those too later.

If you're interested in the process, and how my model differs from a random walk, and where it falls short, I made a YouTube video out of it. It includes a quiz where you try to spot which paths are by real ants and which are by my model. I'd be interested to see how well the model does in that test. Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zz6LKJT3qow

records.title: Show HN: Hormuz Signal – Iran war escalation risk from real data
records.author: mrPaul658
records.storyText:
This is a side project I have started to get hard data on Hormuz Strait escalation risk. Reading the narrative anything can happen from Iran claiming to be ready to open the Strait in a couple days to serious US analysts contemplating the apparently realistic scenario of US using a nuclear warhead to hit Pickaxe Mountain. Basically narrative is too volatile to be trusted.

I figured that focusing on data could be more fruitful. Anything from amount of oil flowing through the Strait every day to US oil reserves to China oil imports can be more informative of the war escalation risk than political narrative. The reality is that politicians make decisions based on real data available to them.

The website tracks over a dozen of such data points, including sensors measuring seismic activity in Iran. So if someone actually hits the Pickaxe Mountain the sensor reading it can be faster than a news report coming out minutes later. Iran testing a bomb would also be visible on the seismic activity readings.

All the data is distilled into a single score measuring Iran war escalation risk. How many carriers does the USA have in the area? How many fighter jets does it have? Is the press coverage of the war increasing or decreasing? Are the oil pipelines open or not? There is a lot of other data. All of that gets combined, weighted and distilled into a single 0-100 score. On this scale, 0 means peace with no issues on the horizon, and 100 means hot war.

In these crazy times, the narrative can be crazy too. It's better to look at hard data and consolidate it into a single score / chart. This will tell you much more about the situation on the ground than listening to the talk will. The site has much more data than this though. Check it out for yourself!

records.title: Show HN: Backuparr – Backups for the *ARR Stack and Plex/Jellyfin/Emby
records.author: rsaturns
records.storyText:
I run the *arr stack on my NAS and like the lazy bad admin I was, didn't backup the configuration files / databases etc. and proceeded to have to set this all up again when my NAS died. Needless to say this sucked. So I got started on a project to ensure I didn't have to go through this again and make it as hands off as possible. I wanted something that would collect backups on a schedule and put them somewhere else, ready in the event the worst strikes again. Doing some scouring I couldn't find anything that addressed this in the manner and scope I was looking for.

Backuparr is a single Docker container with a web UI. You give it each app's URL and API key, choose where the backups go (a local folder, Google Drive, OneDrive or Dropbox, all through rclone), and set a schedule and how long to keep them. It currently supports Radarr, Sonarr, Lidarr, Whisparr, Prowlarr, Profilarr, Bazarr, Tdarr, SABnzbd, NZBGet, Tautulli, Jellyfin, Emby, Plex, Seerr, and LazyLibrarian.

If an app has a backup API, Backuparr uses it. Emby, Plex and Seerr don't have one, so it takes a SQLite online backup of their databases from a mounted folder. All of them except Profilarr can be restored from Backuparr itself, once the service container is re-deployed.

The closest existing tool I found was servarr-backup, which covers Radarr, Sonarr and Prowlarr and sends backups to S3. I wanted more apps and the destinations I actually use.

Limitations: the backup archives themselves aren't encrypted. Only Backuparr's own config (API keys and passwords) and rclone credentials are. Jellyfin, Emby, Plex and Seerr need their folders mounted into the container.

I built this with my coding companion du jour claude-code, along with full review, a lot of self testing, debugging, full lab synthetic tests and running it against my own stack. I’ve been using it for two months now and would love some additional feedback.

Docs: https://rsaturns.github.io/backuparr/ License: AGPLv3

Agents can nowadays design UI very competently, but the wider question of graphic design is largely unsolved.

On one side, you have image models like ChatGPT images, which are high-quality but recognizable and barely editable. On the other hand, you can use LLMs and accept results that, well, look like UI.

I've been working on Rivermark for a few months now to tackle this issue. It's an infinite canvas with an agent that excels at creating on-brand visual content for socials, marketing, and to some extent print. We found it works best for people who are not designers but who know what looks good. MCP features to connect it to your agents are coming soon.

We're powered by superfast inference at almost 1000 tokens per second and a custom realtime harness, meaning the agent is non-blocking and always responsive, and even has a non-turn-based voice mode that you can just talk into.

We have some teams and early power users shipping work with it and are learning a lot. There have been numerous engineering and product challenges to even get here - I'd be happy to talk about them!

records.title: Show HN: OpenPetCam – a self-hosted pet camera that goes looking for your dog
records.author: crimeacs
records.storyText:
I wanted a camera for our dog that didn't stream my living room through a vendor's cloud, and that could answer "where is she?" without me steering a joystick. OpenPetCam is what came out of that.

The camera is a cheap pan/tilt model reflashed with Thingino (open firmware). It dials out over WireGuard to a $5 VPS, so nothing is open on the home network. The server relays WebRTC to your phone, records a rolling 6 hours, and runs the detection.

The part I find interesting is the "is that really her?" problem. YOLOX-nano happily calls a plush toy a dog, so every box goes through a second model, a MobileNetV2 fine-tuned on your own camera's crops. The cut-off is set from the weakest photo of your pet rather than a fixed 0.5: on held-out days a fixed 0.5 let 12 of 25 night lookalikes through, and this rule let none through. A search only says "found her" when 2 of 4 still frames agree. Box plus check is 37 ms on the $5 box, and the whole thing idles at about 5% of one core.

When she's out of view it sweeps the room (saved views first, then the pan rows) and stops on her. There's also an optional agent: tap "Something wrong?" in the app, and Claude Code on your laptop reads the report and the video around it, writes a fix with a test, and ships it only if the tests and a held-out replay pass.

Honest limits: tested on one camera model so far, the setup assumes you can run a VPS, and when she lies right under the camera with her head out of frame the detector still misses her. I'd love to hear from people with other Thingino cameras.

records.title: Show HN: Export your Character.AI chats in minutes – open-source, runs locally
records.author: Amavie
records.storyText:
Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 in October, and the auction of the company is scheduled for November 23. Its built-in data export can take three to four weeks, and the download link expires after seven days. People with years of conversations have been asking how to keep a copy before anything changes.

This is a small browser extension for Chrome and Firefox (Manifest V3). On a character.ai tab you press its button, and it reads your own chats, characters, personas and memory boxes from the site's web API with the session you are already signed in with, one request at a time, and saves one JSON file, plus plain text if you want it. Every line keeps who wrote it and when, which the official export does not.

It asks for no permissions in advance (activeTab and scripting), only reads, talks to nothing but character.ai, and has no analytics or servers. The code in src/ is what runs: nothing is bundled or minified. MIT license.

Disclosure: we make Amavie, an AI character app. We also built a free viewer that opens the file, or the official export ZIP, in the browser without uploading it: https://amavie.ai/character-ai-export. The extension does not need an account with us.

The store listings are in review; until then, unzip the Chrome build from Releases and load it unpacked. Feedback is welcome, especially from very large accounts.

records.title: Show HN: Ifso.io – Plan financial decisions with no sign-in needed
records.author: timer_interrupt
records.storyText:
Hello HN!

I'm a software engineer and a personal finance nerd, and I've spent the past 6 months building Ifso, a planner that shows how your financial decisions play out.

I started Ifso because I wanted to see how a few decisions I was weighing would actually turn out, and the existing tools weren't quite what I was looking for. They were complicated for simple things, and it felt like I had to do a lot of learning just to get off the ground. Beyond that, modeling simple moves (selling a house, changing my monthly contributions from a given year on, etc.) was unexpectedly hard. What I fundamentally wanted was to just tell the simulator "here's what I want to do, how does it end up for me?"

I built Ifso around that philosophy: you enter your finances today, put in the decisions you're looking to make, and see how it plays out and whether you'd be on track to reach your goals. My goal was to make it as easy to use as possible and keep the complexity hidden away, while still giving you as much insight as possible. You can use Ifso without signing in. Nothing to link and no bank login, so everything is typed in by hand, and your plan is saved in your browser. If you want your plans across devices, you can always sign in for free. Your data is never shared, and you have total control over your data, so you can download or delete it at any point if you'd like.

Behind the scenes, the simulation engine handles all of the calculations for you. It automatically runs through investment account growth, loan amortization schedules, income taxes, capital gains, retirement account rules, etc, and then you get a straightforward answer on how the plan works out in the end. You can also run Monte Carlo simulations to stress test a plan, build a second plan with one thing changed and compare the two side by side, and more.

A big part of the user experience is that actions live where you'd expect them. If you want to sell a house in a given year, you go to that house and simulate selling it right there. If you want to increase your retirement savings, that option lives right on the retirement account itself. The same idea carries through the rest of it, where you can convert a property into a rental as an action on the property itself, view a year's cash flow as a visual diagram from that year, or turn a decision on and off to quickly see how it changes things.

If you have any thoughts, suggestions, or any feedback, please let me know. Feedback from users has been an integral part of getting Ifso to where it is today, and I'd love to keep making it more helpful!

Landing page, where you can find a more comprehensive list of features and functionality: https://ifso.io

Try the planner without signing in: https://ifso.io/try
